attacks.claim: The public Recent signers panel prints each confirmed signer's full name and postal code. The agreed rule allows only first name, last initial and city, and for EU signers this is also a GDPR data-minimisation failure. The exposure is visible to anonymous visitors and cannot be recalled once scraped or cached.
The newsletter opt-in is pre-ticked. GDPR Art. 7 requires a clear affirmative act for marketing consent from EU signers, so the default must be unchecked before EU traffic is served.

Validation errors are shown only by red border and background colour. The aria-live paragraph is never written to, and invalid fields get no aria-invalid or aria-describedby association, so screen-reader users are not told which field failed or why. This fails WCAG 3.3.1 (Level A, in scope for AA) and 1.4.1.
attacks.evidence: for (const name of fields) form.elements[name].classList.add('is-invalid'); ...

attacks.claim: The WCAG 2.1 AA claim rests on one automated axe scan of the sign page. That scan does not exercise the error flow, focus movement, or screen-reader announcements, and the Recent panel is not covered either, so conformance for public flows is unsupported.
attacks.evidence: axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations

attacks.claim: The submit handler branches only on 422 and success. A 409 duplicate, a 5xx, or a network failure gives the user no feedback and the button stays enabled. A 422 without a non-empty fields array makes fields[0] undefined and throws.
attacks.evidence: if (res.status === 422) { const { fields } = await res.json(); ... } if (res.ok) window.location = res.headers.get('Location');

attacks.claim: The 409 duplicate-email response reveals whether an address has already signed a petition, which enables enumeration of signers by email. The artifact does not describe a uniform response.
attacks.evidence: Duplicate signature (same email) rejected with 409 | Pass

attacks.claim: The unauthenticated sign endpoint has no stated CSRF token, rate limit, or bot protection. It can be scripted to mass-sign and trigger confirmation emails to third-party addresses, which is also an uncapped Postmark cost vector.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: CSRF token and rate limit on /p/{slug}/sign; only the export is rate-limited. Confirmation emails go through Postmark.

attacks.claim: No retention period, erasure path, or withdrawal mechanism is stated for confirmed signers' personal data, and no removal path exists for a name already shown on the public panel.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention period and erasure path for confirmed signatures; signer removal from Recent signers

attacks.claim: EU signers' emails are sent through a US processor. The artifact cites only a countersigned DPA and a subprocessor listing, and names no transfer mechanism such as SCCs or the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
attacks.evidence: DPA countersigned 2026-09-14, listed in the public subprocessor page.

attacks.claim: Rollback is a flag flip only. It does not address PII already stored, confirmation emails already sent, or names already displayed or cached on public pages, and it is unclear whether the Recent panel sits behind the flag at all.
attacks.evidence: Rollback: flip `petitions_signing` off; sign form is replaced by the existing "Follow this petition" button.

attacks.claim: The 24h watch covers only submit error rate and confirmation bounce rate. It has no privacy-exposure, consent, or 409/422 spike signal, so the 10%-to-100% step can proceed while the panel defect is live.
attacks.evidence: Watch `sign_submit_error_rate` (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%) for 24h. ... Fri 14:00 UTC: 100%.

attacks.claim: The load test covers only signature writes at 400/s. The page-view path (the recent_signers query, 15s polling fan-out, and CDN cache behaviour) is untested, and it is the high-volume path for a viral petition.
attacks.evidence: Load: 400 signatures/s sustained for 10 min, p95 210ms | Pass

attacks.claim: The Recent signers 'Pass' checks the row count and confirmed-only filter, not the displayed fields. It therefore gives no evidence about the agreed name-privacy limit.
attacks.evidence: Recent signers renders 20 most recent confirmed | Pass

attacks.claim: The sign form does not disclose that the organizer receives signer data through CSV export. The export field list is also unspecified, so organizers may receive more than update mailing requires.
attacks.evidence: Organizers can export signers who opted in to updates as CSV; export is rate-limited and audit-logged.

attacks.claim: The artifact does not state that user-supplied full name and city are escaped when rendered on public pages.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: output escaping statement for {{ s.full_name }} and {{ s.city }}

attacks.claim: Confirmation emails have no volume cap or spend ceiling, so a viral petition could produce unbounded Postmark cost.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: email volume cap or budget for confirmations.

attacks.claim: All double opt-in confirmation depends on one US vendor with no stated fallback or exit plan, so a Postmark outage blocks confirmations.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; DPA countersigned 2026-09-14

attacks.claim: The rollout starts Thursday afternoon UTC and moves to 100% on Friday with no stated weekend on-call coverage.
attacks.evidence: Thu 14:00 UTC: flag `petitions_signing` to 10% of petition pages. ... Fri 14:00 UTC: 100%.

attacks.claim: The submit button has no pending state, so a user can double-submit while the fetch is in flight.
attacks.evidence: <button type="submit" class="btn-sign">Sign petition</button> ... const res = await fetch(form.action, ...)
